title: Service-life superlubricity in ordinary machine contacts

concept.text: The proposed innovation is a bearing, gear, or sliding contact that maintains extremely low friction and acceptably low damaging wear throughout representative machine service. The defining capability is endurance: the contact would retain its performance through its intended operating life, rather than merely achieve a low friction coefficient during an initial measurement or a narrowly controlled experiment.

In this concept, ordinary service includes specified exposure to humidity, contamination, misalignment, changing loads, repeated starts and stops, and wear debris. Success would require the complete contact system—including its surfaces, interface treatment, and operating conditions—to tolerate those disturbances while remaining within the machine element’s functional tolerances. This is a proposed engineering capability; the supplied evidence does not establish that it has been achieved.

significance.text: As a conditional engineering assessment, sustaining both very low friction and very low damaging wear could substantially reduce the energy consumed at machine contacts and extend maintenance intervals in equipment whose servicing is driven by contact wear. The revolutionary advance would be making those benefits dependable over useful service lives, so that machine designers could rely on them when selecting drives, contact geometries, and maintenance schedules.

The magnitude of the benefit would depend on how much contact friction contributes to total energy consumption and how strongly wear controls component replacement. Lower contact losses would not eliminate aerodynamic, electrical, or other machine losses. Likewise, suppressing wear would not guarantee infinite machine life: fatigue and other failure mechanisms could still limit service. Longer equipment life and lower operating costs are therefore conditional downstream possibilities, not automatic consequences of a small measured friction coefficient.

missing_breakthrough.text: The missing capability, as defined by this proposal, is reliable preservation of the low-friction interface under a representative service duty cycle. A low initial friction coefficient does not establish that the interface will survive repeated loading, environmental exposure, or progressive surface change. The engineering challenge is to sustain low friction and acceptable wear together, rather than optimize one measurement while leaving durability unresolved.

The proposed barrier set includes maintaining performance despite misalignment and changing loads; tolerating humidity, contamination, and internally generated debris; and surviving starts, stops, and transient overloads. Any specialized interface must remain effective for the claimed service interval without replenishment if that is part of the demonstrated capability. Scaling a contact experiment into a bearing or gear also requires showing that the measured friction benefit produces useful complete-system performance.

These barriers describe the intended research and engineering target. The supplied review found no inspectable scientific content establishing which barriers have already been overcome or documenting their present status across the field. They should therefore be treated as requirements of this proposed capability, rather than as an independently verified inventory of all remaining tribology problems.

current_state.text: The supplied research attributes to Wan Wang, Zijun Ding, Panpan Li, and colleagues a study titled “Engineering-Grade Macroscale Superlubricity Under Ultrahigh Contact Pressure in Atmospheric Air via Multiscale Synergistic Meta-Interfaces,” identified as an Advanced Materials paper published online on 25 March 2026, DOI 10.1002/adma.202520241. It reports a friction coefficient of 0.008 over 100,000 laps at 12.7 GPa contact pressure and 40% relative humidity using engineered interfaces. These bibliographic details and quantitative results are preserved as attributed reports, not independently verified findings.

The research describes the PubMed abstract as its source and states that the full paper was not inspected. However, the supplied review found that the retained artifact contained only a cookie-access screen, with no article identifiers or scientific text. Consequently, that artifact could not verify the study’s identity, publication date, interface design, or numerical results. The source index’s saved-file and verification flags do not resolve this content-access limitation. Missing accessible evidence does not establish that the reported result is false.

If confirmed, the reported combination of low friction, high contact pressure, atmospheric humidity, and 100,000 laps would constitute a substantial contact-scale demonstration. Its scope would still differ from a contaminated bearing or gear operating through a representative service life. The supplied information does not establish endurance in hours, the relationship between laps and machine duty cycles, wear remaining within component tolerances, or complete-system losses. These are limits on the available evidence, not findings that the experiment failed those requirements.

The supplied review also identifies a separate coverage limitation: no bounded search record was provided to assess developments through 1 November 2026. The attributed March 2026 result therefore cannot establish either the latest state of the field or the absence of later service-life demonstrations.

completion_criteria.text: Proposed demonstration: operate a representative bearing or gear pair at its declared design load and speed in humid air with specified contamination, using a predeclared endurance endpoint of at least 1,000 hours or 10⁸ cycles. The protocol should identify which endpoint governs acceptance and define the duty cycle, humidity, contaminant type and concentration, alignment conditions, and permissible wear. These numerical targets are proposed evaluation criteria, not established consensus standards.
completion_criteria.label: Bearing or gear endures ≥1,000 hours or 10⁸ cycles

completion_criteria.text: Proposed acceptance measures: demonstrate a friction coefficient below 0.01 wherever that quantity is meaningfully defined and measurable for the chosen contact, while keeping wear within the component’s original functional tolerances. Specify the measurement method and acceptance interval, and document any running-in period or performance excursions. Complete the endurance test without replenishing a specialized coating, while explicitly describing any other permitted maintenance or lubrication.
completion_criteria.label: Friction below 0.01 within wear tolerances without coating replenishment

completion_criteria.text: Proposed robustness and reproducibility checks: include repeated starts, transient overloads, multiple specimens, and comparison with a conventional contact under matched operating conditions. Compare complete-system losses and service life as well as local friction and wear. Independent reproduction would strengthen confidence that the result is transferable beyond one specimen or laboratory. The outcome should state its demonstrated operating envelope; finite testing can establish breadth across tested conditions, not universal performance in every machine or environment.
completion_criteria.label: Robustness across multiple specimens benchmarked against matched conventional contacts

related_concepts.text: Roster-based comparison: MEC-11, “Transferable prediction of wear and component life,” concerns forecasting degradation and useful life, whereas MEC-02 concerns physically sustaining low friction and low damaging wear. Prediction could help qualify a superlubricious contact or identify its operating limits, but successful prediction alone would not deliver durable superlubricity. The supplied roster supports this broad distinction; MEC-11’s full concept text was not provided for a detailed overlap assessment.

Roster-based comparison: MEC-12, “Predictive mechanics of real, evolving surface contacts,” overlaps with understanding how contact conditions change during service. Such predictive mechanics could support interface design and interpretation of endurance tests. It remains distinct from demonstrating the specific long-lived low-friction capability proposed here.

Roster-based comparison: MEC-04, “Ambient fatigue immunity in bulk structural metals,” and MEC-07, “Bulk structural solids at a large fraction of ideal strength,” address different material-performance limits. A contact that resists wear could still be limited by fatigue or bulk structural failure. These entries therefore remain separate advances rather than consequences of superlubricity.

Conditional application links: MEC-08, “Distributed actuators that simultaneously match skeletal muscle,” and MEC-14, “Low-cost mechanical storage with high efficiency over long periods,” could benefit where contact friction or wear materially limits their performance. Durable superlubricity would address only that contribution; it would not by itself satisfy either concept’s broader performance requirements. These links are inferences from the supplied titles.

unresolved_issues: The attributed paper’s identity, publication details, interface design, and reported coefficient, lap count, pressure, and humidity remain unverified from scientific document content.

The supplied material does not establish the reported experiment’s wear measurements, elapsed endurance time, duty cycle, replenishment requirements, specimen variability, or performance under contamination and service transients.
No bounded search record establishes coverage through 1 November 2026 or identifies subsequent demonstrations.

A concrete completion protocol must select its governing duration endpoint and define the machine element, duty cycle, contamination, friction measurement, wear tolerances, permitted maintenance, and comparison baseline.
Related-concept comparisons are limited to the supplied roster titles; full descriptions, particularly for MEC-11 and MEC-12, would be needed to assess detailed overlap.

brief.title: Machine parts that stay slippery throughout their life
possible: Bearings that support moving parts, gears and sliding surfaces could keep moving with extremely low friction throughout their working life. They would retain that performance through humidity, dirt, changing loads and repeated starts, while keeping wear within the limits needed to function.
why: Machines could use less energy overcoming friction, and equipment whose parts wear out could go longer between maintenance visits. Designers could rely on those savings when choosing drives, moving parts and service schedules.

sources.who: Wan Wang, Zijun Ding, Panpan Li and colleagues
sources.showed: They achieved superlubricity, meaning extremely low friction, using patterned surfaces and protective coatings under high pressure in humid air.
sources.quote: Our findings demonstrate a robust superlubricity regime with a friction coefficient of 0.008
sources.cited_for: The study supports the possibility of sustaining extremely low friction under high pressure and humidity.
sources.not_established: It does not establish a bearing or gear's full working life with contamination, changing loads and acceptable wear.

sources.who: Chanaka Kumara, Michael J. Lance and Jun Qu
sources.showed: They achieved extremely low friction between sliding steel surfaces using a coating of tiny carbon tubes that breaks down during use. A small amount of oil was essential.
sources.quote: Such a superlubricity performance has shown good sustainability in extended testing of more than 500,000 cycles and strong ability of accommodating changes in sliding conditions.
sources.cited_for: The study supports sustained low friction in steel contacts and tolerance of changes in sliding conditions.
sources.not_established: It does not establish service-life performance in a complete bearing or gear under the proposed operating conditions.

shown: Wang and colleagues sustained extremely low friction for 100,000 laps under high pressure in humid air. Kumara and colleagues demonstrated extended steel sliding with an oil-assisted coating. Both are contact experiments; full working-life performance in an ordinary bearing or gear remains to be demonstrated.
missing: A complete bearing or gear must sustain low friction and acceptable wear through a representative working life.
The surfaces must tolerate dirt, wear debris, misalignment, changing loads, starts and overloads together.
The performance must last without replenishing the specialized coating.
Repeated tests must show useful reductions in whole-machine losses and longer service life against conventional contacts.

milestones.label: A bearing or gear completes a representative endurance test
milestones.explanation: A bearing or gear would have to reach at least 1,000 hours or the specified alternative cycle target under declared loads, humidity and contamination. This would connect contact experiments to sustained machine operation.

milestones.label: Low friction persists within wear limits without coating replenishment
milestones.explanation: The friction coefficient, a measure of sliding resistance, would have to stay below 0.01 while wear remains within original functional limits, without coating replenishment. This would establish low friction and durability together.

milestones.label: Repeated specimens outperform matched conventional contacts under service disturbances
milestones.explanation: Multiple specimens would have to withstand repeated starts and overloads, with whole-system losses and service life compared against matched conventional contacts. This would test consistency and practical benefit.

uncertain: The endurance test still needs a governing duration or cycle endpoint and clear rules for operating conditions, wear and permitted maintenance.
How far performance transfers between machines and environments remains open; finite tests establish only the conditions tested.
Independent reproduction would strengthen confidence that the performance extends beyond one laboratory.

page.title: Service-life superlubricity in machine elements
page.definition: A bearing or gear maintains a sliding friction coefficient below 0.01—the ratio of friction force to normal force—through its specified design life, while wear remains within its functional limits. The capability is demonstrated for a named machine element and operating environment.

goal.need: A 2017 global assessment attributed about 23% of world energy consumption to friction and wear. Its breakdown separates energy dissipated by friction from energy used to remanufacture worn components. Sustaining superlubricity targets contact losses over a component's operating life; these sector-wide estimates do not quantify savings attainable by superlubricity.

figures.caption: Estimated global energy use attributed to friction and wear in the 2017 assessment
rows: Remanufacturing worn parts and spare equipment
figures.note: EJ means exajoules. The estimates concern different consequences of tribological contacts.

statements.body: SSLiP, European Innovation Council Pathfinder project
statements.quote: a net friction coefficient of <0.01 operating at 10’s MPa nominal pressure that persists without degradation under boundary lubrication conditions.
statements.context: The project's stated target for macroscale superlubricity; boundary lubrication means the contacting surfaces are not fully separated by a fluid film.

statements.body: Fraunhofer IWM, IWS, IKTS and IPA, SupraSlide project
statements.quote: The challenge is to ensure long-term reliability and temperature stability under practical conditions.
If we reduce friction, we can reduce energy consumption.
statements.context: Jun Qu, leader of the laboratory's Surface Engineering and Tribology group, discussing superlubricity coatings.

completion.title: A machine element retains superlubricity and its wear limits throughout its specified design life.
completion.criterion: A qualified bearing or gear completes its published manufacturer- or customer-specified design life in its intended operating environment, maintaining sliding friction coefficient μ<0.01 after the specified running-in, with wear within the element's existing functional limits. The demonstration covers the application's specified loads, speeds, starts and stops, environmental exposures, alignment tolerances and permitted maintenance. Success applies to that machine element, duty cycle and design life; no universal duration or cycle count is assigned.
completion.set_by: Atlas operational definition; the friction threshold follows tribology usage, and the service-life requirement follows the SSLiP and SupraSlide objectives.
completion.basis: Searches of ISO and ASTM catalogues, SSLiP objectives, SupraSlide publications and machine-contact endurance literature found no combined superlubricity, wear and full-service-life acceptance test. The narrow test joins the field's μ<0.01 convention to a named application's existing design-life and wear requirements. SSLiP specifies persistence but no duration; SupraSlide identifies long-term operation as the goal.

milestones.title: A macroscale sliding contact achieves a measured friction coefficient below 0.01 in the laboratory.
milestones.criterion: Measure sliding μ<0.01 in a macroscale contact. Kumara et al. (2023) report μ=0.001–0.007 for steel–steel sliding with a carbon-nanotube coating and polyalphaolefin oil, with superlubricity sustained for >500,000 cycles. Wang et al., published on 25 March 2026, report μ=0.008 for 100,000 laps at 12.7 GPa contact pressure and 40% relative humidity. These are contact experiments, not completed bearing or gear service lives; neither abstract states specimen counts.
milestones.set_by: Tribology community convention, explicitly stated by Kumara, Lance and Qu in Materials Today Nano.
milestones.threshold_quote: Superlubricity, i.e., coefficient of friction (COF) below 0.01,

milestones.title: Superlubricating technology is demonstrated in an industrially relevant environment (TRL 6).
milestones.criterion: Demonstrate the technology in an industrially relevant environment. Gears: Yilmaz et al., published on 21 August 2019, derived mean gear friction <0.01 over a range of conditions on an FZG gear rig: two test runs, 5-minute operating points and a separate 300-minute temperature test. Plain bearings: Fraunhofer reported an application-oriented axial-bearing test on 23 November 2022, without numerical endurance data (not peer reviewed). These support component-level progress; neither source assigns TRL 6 or establishes design-life performance.
milestones.set_by: European Commission, Horizon 2020 Work Programme 2014–2015, Annex G, TRL 6. This is a generic maturity criterion, applied here to superlubricity.

milestones.title: A superlubricated machine-element prototype works in its operational environment (TRL 7).
milestones.criterion: Demonstrate a system prototype in its operational environment, with the superlubricated contact performing its intended machine function. This is Horizon 2020 TRL 7, a generic maturity test with no prescribed endurance duration or specimen count. The cited gear-rig measurements and axial-bearing application test do not establish operation in an installed machine's intended environment for either case.
milestones.set_by: European Commission, Horizon 2020 Work Programme 2014–2015, Annex G, TRL 7. This is a generic maturity criterion, applied here to superlubricity.
milestones.threshold_quote: system prototype demonstration in operational environment

milestones.title: A complete superlubricated machine-element system passes qualification (TRL 8).
milestones.criterion: Complete and qualify the system against the intended application's requirements. Horizon 2020 TRL 8 requires a complete, qualified system but supplies no superlubricity-specific wear limit, specimen count or endurance duration. It is the qualification stage before the full-design-life operational demonstration used as completion here. No qualification result for either listed case was identified.
milestones.set_by: European Commission, Horizon 2020 Work Programme 2014–2015, Annex G, TRL 8. This is a generic maturity criterion, applied here to superlubricity.

not_found: No external acceptance test combining superlubricity, functional wear limits and a complete machine design life was found.
No adoption of the Horizon 2020 readiness levels as a superlubricity-specific qualification scheme was found.
Specimen counts and elapsed endurance times for the two supplied papers were not available in their accessible abstracts; full experimental protocols were not verified.
No published qualification or full-design-life operational result was found for the listed machine elements.

results.finding: Macroscale contact, sample size not stated, achieved μ=0.008.
results.detail: The contact sustained superlubricity for 100,000 laps at 12.7 GPa and 40% relative humidity. The source does not identify it as a plain bearing.
results.quote: Our findings demonstrate a robust superlubricity regime with a friction coefficient of 0.008 sustained over 100 000 laps under extreme coupled conditions: millimeter-scale contact size, 12.7 GPa contact pressure, and 40% relative humidity.

results.finding: Macroscale contact, sample size not stated, achieved μ=0.008.
results.detail: The contact sustained superlubricity for 100,000 laps at 12.7 GPa and 40% relative humidity. The source does not identify it as a gear.
results.quote: Our findings demonstrate a robust superlubricity regime with a friction coefficient of 0.008 sustained over 100 000 laps under extreme coupled conditions: millimeter-scale contact size, 12.7 GPa contact pressure, and 40% relative humidity.

results.finding: Macroscale steel–steel sliding achieved μ=0.001–0.007; specimen count not stated.
results.detail: A sacrificial carbon-nanotube coating and polyalphaolefin oil were used in ambient conditions. The source reports a contact experiment, not a complete bearing test.
results.quote: Here we present ultra-low COF of 0.001–0.007 by using a sacrificial coating composed of vertically-aligned carbon nanotubes (CNTs) for macroscale steel-steel sliding under minimum quantity lubrication (MQL) of a polyalphaolefin (PAO) oil in the ambient environment.

results.finding: Gear-relevant roller–ring contacts, specimen count unspecified: measured friction coefficient not stated numerically.
results.detail: The study measured friction in macroscale rolling–sliding contacts intended to inform gear applications. The supplied text describes friction reductions but does not state a measured coefficient below 0.01; numerical results are presented in figures.
results.quote:
Overall, the transmission oil performs
better in terms of friction under boundary lubrication at low rolling
speeds, while the glycerol-based lubricants allow to obtain a significant
reduction of friction as the hydrodynamic effects is being enhanced
with the increasing rolling speed.

results.finding: Super-lubricating bearings: sample size not stated; friction coefficients <0.01.
results.detail: Fraunhofer reports that prototypes were tested with industry partners, but does not specify the test environment, operating conditions, endurance or TRL.
results.quote: These well-matched material-lubricant pairings were then used to create super-lubricating bearings. With extremely low friction coefficients of < 0.01, new, virtually loss-free applications were developed across a wide range of systems.

results.finding: Ship-shaft plain-bearing prototypes, three configurations: friction coefficient 0.005 at 1 m/s; sample size not stated.
results.detail: A water-bath rig tested 60 mm bearings at 0.25 MPa, with operating points lasting 0.5 or 1 hour. The source does not establish that the test environment was industrially relevant or demonstrate design-life performance.
results.quote: The friction coefficient curves become 0.005 at a circumferential speed of 1 m/s and thereafter become a constant value regardless of the circumferential speed.

results.finding: EVP PTFE stern-tube bearing, sample size unspecified: bench-test friction coefficient about 0.001.
results.detail: The manufacturer reports class approval for bearing pressure and bearing length, but does not state that the complete system was qualified for superlubricity or report qualification endurance and wear results.
results.quote:
PTFE used for sliding face is well known as 
a low friction material, and even in our 
bench test, it indicated very low friction 
coefficient of about 0.001.
